{{field-1}}"] ["question-144d3b46-ddcf-55fb-8478-125713df09d1" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{6x+1} & ={6}^{x+7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{6x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x+7})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)=(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x & =\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-144d3b46-ddcf-55fb-8478-125713df09d1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde" :answer-field/id #uuid "1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde"] ["answer-87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da" :answer/id #uuid "87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da"] ["answer-87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da" :answer/value "\frac{7\ln(6)-\ln(2)}{6\ln(2)-\ln(6)}"] ["answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde" :answer-field/correct "answer-87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da"] ["answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde" :answer-field/choices "answer-87ff023a-a134-5ecf-9d84-a60f06cfe9da"] ["question-144d3b46-ddcf-55fb-8478-125713df09d1" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-1100e579-fc88-5143-8fa1-3bda713a1cde"] [17592186179789 :knowledge-point/questions "question-144d3b46-ddcf-55fb-8478-125713df09d1"] [17592186180666 :tutorial/content "The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation. 
For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$"] [17592186179885 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0] ["question-f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/id #uuid "f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34"] ["question-f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/math-academy-id "q-152384"] ["question-f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/problem "Simplify $\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}$ given that $z>0.$"] ["question-f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32{z}^{5}}{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{4{z}^{2}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2z)}^{2}} & = \\ |2z| & = \\ |2|\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot |z| & \end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $z>0,$ so we have $|z|=z.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot z & = \\ 2z.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f043c885-cf65-5aa1-b5b8-12a5b94bca34" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-18f8115a-b5d4-5929-a1c8-36a6a9737a96" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "$\sqrt{\frac{9{b}^{4}}{16}}=$"] ["question-ad438bd0-4fe5-5891-83d5-f58699093a97" :question/worked-solution "First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9{b}^{4}}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{(8q)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8|\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot |q|}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $q>0,$ so we have $|q|=q.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot q} & = \\ \frac{3}{8q}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-21c2ef3e-e8f5-5baf-b96b-0dcf270605ef" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e404fc04-8fb2-5959-b21b-6f275023d337" :answer-field/id #uuid the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=3,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{2},$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse."] [17592186162365 :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=3,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={3}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={3}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=3.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=3.$"] [17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$"] [17592186183952 :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) = (x+4)^2 -3$ for $x\geq -4?$"] [17592186183952 :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y = (x+4)^2 -3
$$

:question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=2{x}^{2}-4x+7$ for $x\ge 1.$"] ["question-2079d901-07f2-590c-b43f-09625015f43f" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =2{x}^{2}-4x+7 \\  & =2({x}^{2}-2x)+7 \\  & =2({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2})+7 \\  & =2((x-1)^{2}-1)+7 \\  & =2(x-1)^{2}-2+7 \\  & =2(x-1)^{2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

    

To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y=2(x-1)^{2}+5
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x=2(y-1)^{2}+5
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(y-1)^{2}+5 \\ x-5 & =2(y-1)^{2} \\ \frac{x-5}{2} & =(y-1)^{2} \\ \sqrt{\frac{x-5}{2}} & =y-1 \\ \sqrt{\frac{x-5}{2}}+1 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we selected the positive square root because if $x\ge 1$ is the domain of $f,$ then the range of the inverse is ${f}^{-1}\ge 1.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x)$:

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{x-5}{2}}+1
$$"] ["question-2079d901-07f2-590c-b43f-09625015f43f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0de6a724-f7f8-5dd1-a8c0-8827537e07fb" :answer-field/id #uuid So, to calculate the inverse of a quadratic function, we must first restrict its domain.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic function:

$$
f(x)=(x-2)^2-3
$$

 

Since the function is in vertex form, we can immediately see that the vertex of the corresponding parabola $y=f(x)$ is located at $(2,-3).$ Therefore, the function $f(x)$ will be one-to-one if we restrict its domain to either $x\leq 2$ or $x\geq 2.$ 

Let's restrict the domain to $x\geq 2.$ The graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\geq 2$ is shown below.

![](images/05/059fc0ffddc4b590de8597d3252a6901c7da16063e16b2b4a9a7b24383ce83f7.png)

Now that $f(x)$ is one-to-one, we can calculate its inverse. We follow the four usual steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y.$

$$
y = (x-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y.$

$$
x = (y-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(y-2)^{2}-3 \\ x+3 & =(y-2)^{2} \\ \sqrt{x+3} & =y-2 \\ \sqrt{x+3}+2 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The *domain* of the original function is the *range* of the inverse function. In our case, since the domain of $f$ is $x \geq 2,$ the range of the inverse must be $f^{-1} \geq 2.$ Therefore, we select the positive square root in the third step above. Indeed, notice that $\sqrt{x + 3} +2 \geq 2.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x).$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x + 3} +2
$$

cosine and sine ratios for *acute* angles can be defined in the following ways:

- Using a right triangle. If $\theta$ is an acute angle in a right triangle, then

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}.
$$

- Using the unit circle. If $\theta$ is a central angle made by a point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle in the first quadrant, then

$$
\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y.
$$

We can't define trigonometric ratios for non-acute angles using right triangles because a right triangle can't have angles larger than $90^\circ.$ However, we can *extend* these ratios for non-acute angles using unit circles.

To do that, let's consider the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ in any quadrant, measured in the usual way.

![](images/61/612d468ea23fefb6bbb33bd676a1930604b283475f36be08541419776bb580bd.png)

We *define* the sine and cosine of $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y
$$

In other words, 

- the cosine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $x$-coordinate of $P,$ and

- the sine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $y$-coordinate of $P.$

This way, our trigonometric ratios make sense for any angle, even if this angle is larger than $90^\circ.$"] [17592186060861 :tutorial/content "We can use reference angles to evaluate trigonometric ratios for angles outside the first quadrant. 

To demonstrate, let's determine the value of $\cos (135^\circ),$ corresponding to the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the unit circle, as shown below.

![](images/be/bef50a070785e4bb86867ba6404942fd7eaa04b60720adfb04176bafe2fa2121.png)

The reference angle for $\theta=135^\circ$ is $\theta_R=45^\circ.$ Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/33/33b208e44aaa556a67ebaf7a6c1117b09adf863c56deb1bc1f5590e289062c4b.png)

Let $P'$ be the image of $P$ under a reflection across the $y$-axis. This gives a pair of congruent angles of measure $45^\circ,$ as shown.

![](images/c4/c4875682498edaadc74a8af238fdf3293b4820025256df78e60867940061785e.png)

According to the definition, $\cos(135^\circ)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the point $P.$ But this is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point $P'$ *taken with the opposite sign.* 

The $x$-coordinate of $P'$ equals the cosine of the reference angle. 

$$
\cos(45^\circ)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\cos(\, \underbrace{135^\circ}_{\theta} \,) = - \cos(\, \underbrace{45^\circ}_{\theta_R} \,) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

So, we simplified the evaluation of $\cos(135^\circ)$ by evaluating the cosine of the corresponding reference angle $\theta_R=45^\circ$ *with an additional sign adjustment* for the final result. 

We can use a similar argument to show that, since $y = \sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\sin(135^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.
$$

In this case, we do **NOT** change the sign because the $y$-coordinates of $P'$ and $P$ *are equal.*"] [17592186060972 :tutorial/content "We can calculate a trigonometric ratio of *any* angle $\theta$ by finding the ratio of the corresponding reference angle and adjusting the sign depending on which quadrant our angle lies in.

To do this, we perform the following steps:

1\. Find the reference angle $\theta_R.$

2\. Calculate the value of the ratio for $\theta_R.$

3\. Determine whether the resulting ratio is positive or negative.

We must do the last step because the ratio for $\theta_R$ will always be nonnegative, but the ratio for $\theta$ may not be.

But how do we determine whether the ratio for $\theta$ is positive or negative? This depends on the trigonometric ratio and which quadrant the angle is in.

To help us remember when various trigonometric ratios are positive, we use the mnemonic "**A**ll **S**tudents **T**ake **C**alculus." 

- **A**ll of the trigonometric ratios are positive in quadrant I

- **S**ine (and only sine) is positive in quadrant II

- **T**angent (and only tangent) is positive in quadrant III

- **C**osine (and only cosine) is positive in quadrant IV

We can represent this in a so-called CAST diagram, shown below.

![](images/9a/9a6d43985058f1afd33272537def49886177aceab115f0084b1cf9d08ba78c43.png)

For example, let's consider $\sin 140^\circ.$

**Step 1**: Since $\theta = 140^\circ$ is the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & ={180}^{∘}-\theta  \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{140}^{∘} \\  & ={40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\sin{140^\circ},$ and therefore we're interested in $\sin\theta_R = \sin{40^\circ}.$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\sin{140^\circ}$ must be *positive* because the sine ratio is *always* positive in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin 140^\circ = \sin{40^\circ}.
$$

$\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -\dfrac{\cos\theta + 2\cos(2\theta)}{\sin\theta + 2\sin(2\theta)}$."] [17592186184078 :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P$, we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -\dfrac{\cos\theta + 2\cos(2\theta)}{\sin\theta + 2\sin(2\theta)}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P$.

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{θ = π/2} \\
&= - (\cos (\frac{π}{2}) + 2\cos (π))/(\sin (\frac{π}{2}) + 2\sin (π)) \\
&= - (0 + 2(-1))/(1 + 2(0)) \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1} &= r\cos θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos θ)\cos θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\cos (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= (1 + 2 \cdot 0) \cdot 0 \\
&= 0 \\
y_{1} &= r\sin θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos θ)\sin θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\sin (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= (1 + 2 \cdot 0) \cdot 1 \\
&= 1 \cdot 1 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,1)$.

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - 1 &= 2(x - 0) \\
y &= 2x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y'(\theta) = \cos\theta-2\cos(2\theta), \qquad x'(\theta) = 2\sin(2\theta) - \sin\theta
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= (y^{′}(θ))/(x^{′}(θ)) \\
&= (\cos θ - 2\cos (2θ))/(2\sin (2θ) - \sin θ)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P$.

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{θ = 3π/2} \\
&= ((\cos (\frac{3π}{2}) - 2\cos (2 \cdot \frac{3π}{2})))/((2\sin (2 \cdot \frac{3π}{2}) - \sin (\frac{3π}{2}))) \\
&= ((\cos (\frac{3π}{2}) - 2\cos (3π)))/((2\sin (3π) - \sin (\frac{3π}{2}))) \\
&= (0 - 2(-1))/(0 - (-1)) \\
&= \frac{0 + 2}{0 + 1} \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1} &= r\cos θ \\
&= (1 - 2\cos θ)\cos θ \\
&= (1 - 2\cos (\frac{3π}{2}))\cos (\frac{3π}{2}) \\
&= (1 - 2 \cdot 0) \cdot 0 \\
&= 0 \\
y_{1} &= r\sin θ \\
&= (1 - 2\cos θ)\sin θ \\
&= (1 - 2\cos (\frac{3π}{2}))\sin (\frac{3π}{2}) \\
&= (1 - 2 \cdot 0) \cdot (-1) \\
&= 1 \cdot (-1) \\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are

$$
\left(0, -1 \right)
$$

$$

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

as well as the common logarithm ([math]\log[/math]) or the natural logarithm ([math]\ln[/math]) on both sides of our equation to get rid of the exponents."] [17592186162365 :question/problem "A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=3,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{2},$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse."] [17592186162365 :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse ${Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=3,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={3}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax{‖}^{2}}={3}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax‖}=3.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=3.$"] [17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$

$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$"] [17592186183952 :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) = (x+4)^2 -3$ for $x\geq -4$?"] [17592186183952 :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

So, to calculate the inverse of a quadratic function, we must first restrict its domain.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic function:

$$
f(x)=(x-2)^2-3
$$

Since the function is in vertex form, we can immediately see that the vertex of the corresponding parabola $y=f(x)$ is located at $(2,-3)$. Therefore, the function $f(x)$ will be one-to-one if we restrict its domain to either

$$
x\leq 2
$$

or

$$
x\geq 2
$$

Let's restrict the domain to

$$
x\geq 2
$$

The graph of $y=f(x)$ for

$$
x\geq 2
$$

is shown below.

![](images/05/059fc0ffddc4b590de8597d3252a6901c7da16063e16b2b4a9a7b24383ce83f7.png)

Now that $f(x)$ is one-to-one, we can calculate its inverse. We follow the four usual steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$.

$$
y = (x-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$.

$$
x = (y-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (y - 2)^{2} - 3 \\
x + 3 &= (y - 2)^{2} \\
\sqrt{x + 3} &= y - 2 \\
\sqrt{x + 3} + 2 &= y
\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The *domain* of the original function is the *range* of the inverse function. In our case, since the domain of $f$ is

$$
x \geq 2
$$

the range of the inverse must be

$$
f^{-1} \geq 2
$$

Therefore, we select the positive square root in the third step above. Indeed, notice that

$$
\sqrt{x + 3} +2 \geq 2
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$.

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x + 3} +2
$$

We're done!"] [17592186059389 :question/problem "![](images/92/925a47f324868fb022b51ff490ccecc557e989054253ad643542a478deb094d7.png)

$$"] [17592186059390 :question/worked-solution "To express $\sin{335^\circ}$ in terms of $\sin\theta_R$, we follow three steps:

- Using a right triangle. If $\theta$ is an acute angle in a right triangle, then
$\cos\theta = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}$.
- Using the unit circle. If $\theta$ is a central angle made by a point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle in the first quadrant, then
$\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y$.

We can't define trigonometric ratios for non-acute angles using right triangles because a right triangle can't have angles larger than $90^\circ$. However, we can *extend* these ratios for non-acute angles using unit circles.

To do that, let's consider the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ in any quadrant, measured in the usual way.

![](images/61/612d468ea23fefb6bbb33bd676a1930604b283475f36be08541419776bb580bd.png)

We *define* the sine and cosine of $\theta$, as follows:

$$
\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y
$$

In other words,

- the cosine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $x$-coordinate of $P$, and
- the sine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $y$-coordinate of $P$.

This way, our trigonometric ratios make sense for any angle, even if this angle is larger than $90^\circ$."] [17592186060861 :tutorial/content "We can use reference angles to evaluate trigonometric ratios for angles outside the first quadrant.

To demonstrate, let's determine the value of $\cos (135^\circ)$, corresponding to the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the unit circle, as shown below.

![](images/be/bef50a070785e4bb86867ba6404942fd7eaa04b60720adfb04176bafe2fa2121.png)

The reference angle for

$$
\theta=135^\circ
$$

is

$$
\theta_R=45^\circ
$$

Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/33/33b208e44aaa556a67ebaf7a6c1117b09adf863c56deb1bc1f5590e289062c4b.png)

Let $P'$ be the image of $P$ under a reflection across the $y$-axis. This gives a pair of congruent angles of measure $45^\circ$, as shown.

![](images/c4/c4875682498edaadc74a8af238fdf3293b4820025256df78e60867940061785e.png)

According to the definition, $\cos(135^\circ)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$. But this is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point $P'$ *taken with the opposite sign.*

The $x$-coordinate of $P'$ equals the cosine of the reference angle.

$$
\cos(45^\circ)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\cos(\, \underbrace{135^\circ}_{\theta} \,) =-\cos(\, \underbrace{45^\circ}_{\theta_R} \,) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

So, we simplified the evaluation of $\cos(135^\circ)$ by evaluating the cosine of the corresponding reference angle

$$
\theta_R=45^\circ
$$

*with an additional sign adjustment* for the final result.

We can use a similar argument to show that, since

$$
y = \sin\theta
$$

we have

$$
\sin(135^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}
$$

In this case, we do **NOT** change the sign because the $y$-coordinates of $P'$ and $P$ *are equal.*"] [17592186060972 :tutorial/content "We can calculate a trigonometric ratio of *any* angle $\theta$ by finding the ratio of the corresponding reference angle and adjusting the sign depending on which quadrant our angle lies in.

To do this, we perform the following steps:

1. Find the reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the ratio for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting ratio is positive or negative.

We must do the last step because the ratio for $\theta_R$ will always be nonnegative, but the ratio for $\theta$ may not be.

But how do we determine whether the ratio for $\theta$ is positive or negative? This depends on the trigonometric ratio and which quadrant the angle is in.

To help us remember when various trigonometric ratios are positive, we use the mnemonic "**A**ll **S**tudents **T**ake **C**alculus."

- **A**ll of the trigonometric ratios are positive in quadrant I
- **S**ine (and only sine) is positive in quadrant II
- **T**angent (and only tangent) is positive in quadrant III
- **C**osine (and only cosine) is positive in quadrant IV

We can represent this in a so-called CAST diagram, shown below.

![](images/9a/9a6d43985058f1afd33272537def49886177aceab115f0084b1cf9d08ba78c43.png)

For example, let's consider $\sin 140^\circ$.

![](images/da/da7ca1a89b91d157ad97a3800d8c2d67efb467a8ceaa8f3c964bea5275ecfc5d.png)

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = 140^\circ
$$

is the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= 180^{∘} - θ \\
&= 180^{∘} - 140^{∘} \\
&= 40^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\sin{140^\circ}$, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\sin\theta_R = \sin{40^\circ}
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\sin{140^\circ}$ must be *positive* because the sine ratio is *always* positive in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin 140^\circ = \sin{40^\circ}
$$

Let's see another example."]]}

$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P$.

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{θ = π/2} \\
&= - (\cos (\frac{π}{2}) + 2\cos (π))/(\sin (\frac{π}{2}) + 2\sin (π)) \\
&= - (0 + 2(-1))/(1 + 2(0)) \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= (1 + 2\cos θ)\cos θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\cos (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= (1 + 2 \cdot 0) \cdot 0 \\
&= 0 \\
y_{1} &= r\sin θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos θ)\sin θ \\
&= (1 + 2\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\sin (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= (1 + 2 \cdot 0) \cdot 1 \\
&= 1 \cdot 1 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,1)$.

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - 1 &= 2(x - 0) \\
y &= 2x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

The polar curve shown above is defined as

$$
r(\theta) = 4 - 3\cos \theta, \qquad 0\leq \theta < 2\pi
$$

We have

$$
\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

at the point $P$. The tangent to the curve at $P$ is shown in the diagram.

To find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at $P$, we follow four steps.

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

Using techniques that we've previously discussed, we can show that

$$
y^{′}(θ) = 4\cos θ - 3\cos 2θ, x^{′}(θ) = 3\sin 2θ - 4\sin θ
$$

Therefore, we can find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= (y^{′}(θ))/(x^{′}(θ)) \\
&= \frac{4\cos θ - 3\cos 2θ}{3\sin 2θ - 4\sin θ}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P$.

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{θ = π/2} \\
&= (4\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - 3\cos (2 \cdot \frac{π}{2}))/(3\sin (2 \cdot \frac{π}{2}) - 4\sin (\frac{π}{2})) \\
&= (4\cos (\frac{π}{2}) - 3\cos (π))/(3\sin (π) - 4\sin (\frac{π}{2})) \\
&= \frac{0 + 3}{0 - 4} \\
&=-\frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1} &= r\cos θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos θ)\cos θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\cos (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= 0 \\
y_{1} &= r\sin θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos θ)\sin θ \\
&= (4 - 3\cos (\frac{π}{2}))\sin (\frac{π}{2}) \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are

$$
\left(0, 4 \right)
$$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - 4 &= -\frac{3}{4} \cdot (x - 0) \\
y &= -\frac{3}{4}x + 4
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "febc7b49-9662-5e78-a7a5-cbe9b1f596ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6186 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a1e51e4b-71cf-5749-aae1-c001b3a5a59b" :step/math-academy-id 37501 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184944}}] :activity/title "Tangent and Normal Lines to Polar Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184419} {:db/id 17592186185006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

$$

$$

$$
{t}^{2}-22t+121.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-22t+{11}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2\cdot 11t+{11}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=11.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-11)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186507455 :question/id #uuid "85b0de0c-7078-58c3-80c6-e70c35748f20" :question/math-academy-id "q-3001" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ca67fe0-cf38-599e-96f0-f21b24a8ed45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2e+9)^{2}" :db/id 17592186506700} {:answer/id #uuid "1e211f2a-503f-53ec-afa6-8cc382355c12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(e-9)^{2}" :db/id 17592186506739} {:answer/id #uuid "836e756a-76b5-5f29-86b1-a991836e11bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(e-3)^{2}" :db/id 17592186506970} {:answer/id #uuid "c6a4827a-5dc1-5018-8b60-d93186610d52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(e+9)^{2}" :db/id 17592186507110} {:answer/id #uuid "c91d77da-831a-57b5-a1ac-15897539bebc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2e-9)^{2}" :db/id 17592186507117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506739} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8ac7d31-1c83-57d9-9043-68e47336ef2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507373}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Factor the expression ${e}^{2}-18e+81.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Factor ${x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}-2ax+{a}^{2}=(x-a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=\frac{1}{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186507442 :question/id #uuid "5e023823-cd56-5877-8c6f-e730b2d09ff6" :question/math-academy-id "q-78924" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "31315a0d-2c0e-5f94-a1ff-4b7faeb27a09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186506794} {:answer/id #uuid "3701d3f2-5410-556e-b0a7-75420b9f36b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186506810} {:answer/id #uuid "374322ff-4086-5b83-87ee-c3122f61bd52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x+3)}^{2}" :db/id 17592186506811} {:answer/id #uuid "c0be764b-beb0-5776-8b10-64f11f6978bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186507101} {:answer/id #uuid "d9c7dbd4-3ec1-54d0-8413-03bba2ac8751" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186507149}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506794} :answer-field/id #uuid "8adb6eba-9169-5d39-b01b-4fde7ef436d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "${x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{16}=$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

17592186045485} :question/problem "The shoulder height of a moose $h$ measures $2.1\,\text{m}$ to the nearest tenth of a meter. Determine the upper and lower bounds of this measurement." :question/worked-solution "Our measurement is given to the nearest $0.1\,\text{m}.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\frac{0.1\,\text{m}}{2}=0.05\,\text{m}.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =2.1\,\text{m}-0.05\,\text{m} \\  & =2.05\,\text{m} \\ \text{upper bound} & =2.1\,\text{m}+0.05\,\text{m} \\  & =2.15\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $h$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
2.05\,\text{m}\le h<2.15\,\text{m}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138753 :question/id #uuid "aa0fbe16-9c2a-5cfb-9ced-d072cc5a440e" :question/math-academy-id "q-218714" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186138388 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e99cabd4-b713-50e1-83be-f8571b575803" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Bounds When Rounding to a Decimal Place"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "b4e4318f-48a8-53c6-99cd-662866f667a9" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186135517} {:answer-field/id #uuid "7ed79917-ae5a-54e2-98a4-9e0cb7ff5a5f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186135518}] :question/problem "The volume $v$ of acid in a test tube measures $10.25mL$ to the nearest hundredth of a milliliter. Increasing by $9.5%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+9.5%=109.5%=1.095
$$

Now, we multiply the original price by $1.095:$

$$

\begin{aligned}{2}^{4} & =16 \\ {2}^{3} & =8 \\ {2}^{2} & =4 \\ {2}^{1} & =2 \\ {2}^{0} & =◻\,?\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have 

$$
2^{\color{red}{0}}  = {\color{blue}{2}}\div 2 = 1.

In this lesson, we will explore how to quantify and describe measurement errors.

Suppose that a particular rope measures precisely $48.9\,\textrm{cm}.$ Now, imagine we take a meterstick and record a measurement of $50\,\textrm{cm}$ *to the nearest $10$ centimeters*. Let's mark this approximation on our meterstick.

![](images/4e/4e5d5ca05f27aa612b3fdcc9430b495870ddf540630857b6227897d6b20c9e89.png)

The error of a measurement equals the difference between the rounded estimate and the "true" value. So, in this example, the error of our approximation equals

$$
50\,\textrm{cm} - 48.9\,\textrm{cm} = 1.1\textrm{cm}.
$$

  

We often don't know the "true" measurement in practical problems. So, the next best thing is to determine a **lower bound** and an **upper bound** for our measurement:

- The *lower* bound of a measurement is its *smallest* possible value.

- The *upper* bound of a measurement is its *largest* possible value.

Let's figure out the lower and upper bounds of our $50\,\textrm{cm}$ approximation:

- The *lower bound* is $45 \, \textrm{cm}$ because this is the *smallest* value that gives $50 \, \textrm{cm}$ when rounded to the nearest $10\,\textrm{cm}.$

![](images/da/da9cd6208cef81c6fe34fbba9b4271fa3ce1f30df69eb3c631ce6fea4f12e3a3.png)

- The *upper bound* is $55 \, \textrm{cm}$ because this is (almost) the *largest* value that gives $50 \, \textrm{cm}$ when rounded to the nearest $10\,\textrm{cm}.$

![](images/23/23a195d88326b587e1864ef04e7b05f74d675f1ddc987baa2cf586af599eb4a9.png)

Let's use the letter $l$ to denote the "true" length of the rope. Then, we can combine our lower and upper bound measurements into a single statement, as follows:

$$
45\,\textrm{cm} \leq l \lt 55\,\textrm{cm}
$$

Notice that we used a *strict* "<" inequality for the upper bound. We cannot include $55\textrm{cm}$ in our set of values because this number rounds to $60\,\textrm{cm},$ not $50\,\textrm{cm}$.

We can visualize the lower and upper bounds on our diagram as follows:

![](images/1f/1fdacb0787e8316a78da1ad65aa177e9a6f29215fa0d53aef88b0eb33326218d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "d44fcde5-ad8a-596b-a6ac-955ff40b6bd9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8751 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cc0c262d-dd9e-52a1-a83b-9f1c0fe96262" :step/math-academy-id 165169 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139295}} {:db/id 17592186139295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139716 :tutorial/content "So, we've seen how to calculate lower and upper bounds. Before we consider another example, note the following:

- The lower and upper bound depend on our approximation's **degree of accuracy**.

- In the last example, the degree of accuracy was $10\,\textrm{cm}$ because the rope was measured to the nearest $10$ centimeters.

- If we change the degree of accuracy, the lower and upper bounds will also change. So, for example, if we measured the rope to the nearest $1\,\textrm{cm},$ the lower and upper bounds would be different.

- The **greatest possible error** is the largest amount the "true" value can be from the approximation.

- This greatest possible error is always one-half of the degree of accuracy. So, in the last example, the greatest possible error in our measurement was

$$
\dfrac{10\,\textrm{cm}}{2} = {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}}.
$$

We can use the greatest possible error to compute the lower and upper bounds quickly:

- To compute the lower bound of an approximation, we *subtract* the greatest possible error from the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have

$$
\textrm{lower bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} - {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 45\,\textrm{cm.}
$$

- To compute the upper bound of an approximation, we *add* the greatest possible error to the approximation. So, for the previous example, we have

$$
\textrm{upper bound} = 50\,\textrm{cm} + {\color{blue}{5\,\textrm{cm}}} = 55\,\textrm{cm.}
$$

than* a given amount. This corresponds to applying a so-called **percentage increase.**

To apply a percentage increase, we add the increase to $100\%,$ convert the result to a decimal multiplier, and then find the product of the multiplier and the original number.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following problem.

What number is $25\%$ *greater than* $160?$

The key words here are "$\boldsymbol{25\%}$ **greater than.**" This means we need to apply a percentage increase, increasing the original number by $25\%.$

To find a number $25\%$ greater than $160,$ we apply a new percentage of

$$
100\% + 25\% = 125\%.
$$

This means that our new number is $125\%$ of $160.$ 

So, first, we convert this percentage to a decimal:

$$
125\% = \dfrac{125}{100} = 1.25
$$

To find a number that is $25\%$ greater than $160,$ we multiply $160$ by $1.25{:}$

$$
1.25 \cdot 160 = 200
$$

Therefore, the number that is $25\%$ *greater than* $160$ is $200.$

This method applies to *any* percentage increase, including those greater than $100\%{;}$ add the increase to $100\%$ before converting to a decimal multiplier." :tutorial/id #uuid "83dbd64f-3ab9-5239-b54b-ae6d91816248" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14336 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "547ba33b-b6b3-5bae-b2dc-eacefe1e81a4" :step/math-academy-id 615692 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153299}} {:db/id 17592186153299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152295 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151899 :question/id #uuid "2cfd1ed7-8249-5970-9ddc-1bb69929951c" :question/math-academy-id "e-21450"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "125ed0b3-14ad-5af8-8370-ca6f83d93c35" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050716}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152552} {:db/id 17592186152553} {:db/id 17592186455458} {:db/id 17592186455469}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying a Percentage Increase"} :step/id #uuid "a946c7fa-5aee-54d2-b223-0a3b560b3401" :step/math-academy-id 615693 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153300}} {:db/id 17592186153300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152296 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151900 :question/id #uuid "95c3dedd-accd-57dc-91ee-4ee8fdb2f3a4" :question/math-academy-id "e-21451"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f90ea994-79f2-5409-bf96-306803b4ef01" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049467}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152554} {:db/id 17592186152555} {:db/id 17592186455451} {:db/id 17592186455478} {:db/id 17592186455495} {:db/id 17592186455498} {:db/id 17592186486395} {:db/id 17592186486445} {:db/id 17592186534011}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying a Percentage Increase: Word Problems"} :step/id #uuid "fd57418f-a99a-5c17-9192-9191eca0084b" :step/math-academy-id 615696 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153301}} {:db/id 17592186153301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153340 :tutorial/content "It's possible to increase a number by $100\%$ or more.

"d49a6c77-a56c-5955-b68f-69307587aa23" :topic/math-academy-id 352} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065232 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065341 :tutorial/content "A **perfect square trinomial** is a three-term expression that is the result of squaring a binomial.

For example, the expression

$$
x^2 + 6x + 9
$$

is a perfect square trinomial because it is the result of squaring the binomial $(x+3)$, as shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}+6x+9 & \end{aligned}
$$

To factor a perfect square trinomial, we have to figure out what binomial it is the square of. We can often do this by relating the perfect square trinomial to the **square of a sum**:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}2}  {\color{blue}a}x + {\color{blue}a}^2 = (x + {\color{blue}a})^2
$$

 

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $x^2+6x+9$ using the square of sum formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write the constant term as a perfect square:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Factor the trinomial using the "square of a sum formula". In this case, we have ${\color{blue}{a}}={\color{blue}{3}}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

This method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial. We will learn more general methods in the future." :tutorial/id #uuid "c04b9f03-f29f-5feb-8d13-7de9fc378a34" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1596 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$
{e}^{2}-2ae+{a}^{2}=(e-a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{e}^{2}-18e+81.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2}-18e+{9}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2}-2\cdot 9e+{9}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=9.$ This gives

"q-78924" :question/problem "${x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{16}=$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}+2ax+{a}^{2}=(x+a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{16}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=\frac{3}{4}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "840aef68-9d30-531e-8a4f-9c7f5eaf1292" :step/next {:db/id 17592186507555}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "31315a0d-2c0e-5f94-a1ff-4b7faeb27a09" :answer/type {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 239} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060770 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060969 :tutorial/content "Consider the region below, which represents the inequality $2 < x < 5.$

![](images/fe/feeae0bfa9b29e6f034a3fd33d1e9fbd369840835af2d6588892ee6edc2fa120.png)

We can represent this inequality using **interval notation** as follows:

$$
(2,5)
$$

The parentheses $(\phantom{0})$ tell us that the endpoints $x=2$ and $x=5$ are *not* included in this interval.

When an interval does not include the endpoints, we say that it is **open**. 

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (2,5).
$$

The symbol $\in$ means "lies in" or "belongs to." To find the additive inverse of a number, we change its sign by placing a minus symbol $({\color{red}{-}})$ in front of it. 

For example, to find the additive inverse of $5,$ we obtain 

$$
{\color{red}{-}}\,(5) = -5.
$$

To check our work, we add the inverse to the original number. If we're correct, we should get zero.

$$
5+(-5) = 5-5 = 0 \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "21fd73d9-f9b8-5ef8-9e18-9ba21d6d8d79" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15159 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c1f41837-dee8-5f07-9c9f-5cfaebd69d2e" :step/math-academy-id 620103 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074776}} {:db/id 17592186074776 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073437 :question/id #uuid "735e0a05-bc90-5b18-b096-d51d9f9c50e3" :question/math-academy-id "e-22709"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d7d26bc9-6f89-5da4-b8a9-6be6f4280f81" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050421}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074498} {:db/id 17592186074499} {:db/id 17592186445907} {:db/id 17592186445912} {:db/id 17592186533988}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Additive Inverse of a Positive Integer"} :step/id #uuid "6255e96d-283e-52d1-815a-3ba256caf351" :step/math-academy-id 620104 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074777}} {:db/id 17592186074777 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075030 :tutorial/content "To find the additive inverse of a negative number, we can use the same process.

The *distance* between the number $-3$ and $0$ is known as the **absolute value** of $-3.$ We write it as

$$
|-3| = {\color{red}3}.
$$

Similarly, $|\,2\,|$, the absolute value of the number $2$, is the distance between $2$ and $0$:

![](images/f4/f44fcd05fb0932083d48c8b11892247d8de8fbc46ccf7186fb12843702181aea.png)

We write $|\,2\,| = {\color{red}2}.$

So, the absolute value simply 

- *removes the minus sign*, if the number is negative, or

- does nothing, if the number is non-negative.

Sometimes, we can be asked to evaluate an expression involving the absolute value function, like $|x +1| + 5$ when $x=-3.$ In this case, we evaluate the expression inside the absolute value before simplifying the rest of the expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+1|+5 & = \\ |(-3)+1|+5 & = \\ |-2|+5 & = \\ 2+5 & = \\ 7 & \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3325f9a7-d389-562e-ac1b-4eb26671f84b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8817 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2ecbe2d3-3bf6-5c94-9e47-13b35a557d38" :step/math-academy-id :step/content {:db/id 17592186056009 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose that we want to solve an equation like 

$$
\dfrac x 6 = 4.
$$

For this, we can use the **multiplication principle.** The multiplication principle tells us that multiplying (or dividing) both sides of an equation by the same number does not change its solution.

In this case, the variable $x$ is being *divided* by $6.$ To isolate $x$, we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *multiplying* by $6$. So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6.$

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac x 6 					&= 4 \[5pt]
		{\color{blue}{6}} \cdot \dfrac x 6  	&= {\color{blue}{6}}\cdot 4\[5pt]
		\dfrac{6x}{6}			&=24\[5pt]
	}
$$

 

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $6$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac{6x}{6}			&=24 \
		\dfrac{ \cancel{6} x}{\cancel{6} }			&=24 \
		x				&=24
	}
$$

 

Thus, our solution is $x=24.$ Let's check that this solution is correct by plugging it back into the original equation:

$$
\eqalign{
    		\dfrac x 6 &=4 \[5pt]
    		\dfrac{24}{6} &=4 \[5pt]
		4 &= 4 \; {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
	}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "66f28923-eb93-5bc0-b870-b4316258a3c8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8052 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "85cdcdec-1c60-5ac5-8e3f-e25e47c0bb28" :step/math-academy-id 72101 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055884}} {:db/id 17592186055884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054834 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054381 :question/id #uuid "c64cd16e-2f9d-5564-8d04-eddcad2c5d01" :question/math-academy-id "e-12859"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4007f63e-0a99-57ca-a1f6-190b21f02ecc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050414} {:db/id 17592186050599}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055151} {:db/id 17592186055443} {:db/id 17592186479855} {:db/id 17592186479893}] :knowledge-point/title "Linear Equations Requiring Multiplication by a Positive Integer"} :step/id #uuid "036eee4c-d08b-5bac-82ff-0d8314f256ca" :step/math-academy-id 72102 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055885}} {:db/id 17592186055885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054835 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054388 :question/id #uuid "cbce1708-81ba-5d37-ae21-fc8d94ebbc2f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12894"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b765f7b2-639a-5519-9170-02a4fcb0f8fe" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186054940} {:db/id 17592186055290} {:db/id 17592186479828} {:db/id 17592186479865}] :knowledge-point/title "Cases Where the Variable Is on the Right-Hand Side"} :step/id #uuid "f810611a-c93d-5ca0-8ad1-26bd885d89c1" :step/math-academy-id 72105 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055886}} {:db/id 17592186055886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056010 :tutorial/content "In order to remove a negative sign from our variable, we can multiply both sides by $-1$. This way, the two negatives will cancel out to form a positive. 

For example, suppose that we have the equation

$$
-x = 3
$$

We can isolate $x$ by multiplying both sides of the equation by $-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =3 \\ (-1)\cdot (-x) & =(-1)\cdot 3 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the equation is $x=-3.$ Let's check to see that this works by substituting our solution back into the original equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =3 \\ -(-3) & =3 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7de479d1-5bb2-5cc9-9fdc-117a02790cab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8053 :tutorial/title "Removing a Negative Sign from a Variable"} :step/id #uuid "91e35f06-1502-52eb-91c6-d755a826ebfc" :step/math-academy-id 72108 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055887}} {:db/id 17592186055887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054836 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054382 :question/id #uuid "5fe35108-2fa8-563e-862e-ad27d4ed5334" :question/math-academy-id "e-12860"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "712bc4c6-aeaf-5081-9e64-791027b38963" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049349}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055291} {:db/id 17592186055420} {:db/id 17592186479831} {:db/id 17592186479882} {:db/id 17592186538937}] :knowledge-point/title "Linear Equations Requiring Multiplication by a Negative Integer"} :step/id #uuid "fe58020e-d340-5fac-88b2-1c50209326d9" :step/math-academy-id 72109 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055888}} {:db/id 17592186055888 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056011 :tutorial/content "To solve an equation like $7x = 21$, we again need to look at what's happening to the variable and ask ourselves what the opposite operation is.

In this case, the variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $7.$ To isolate $x$, we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $7$. So, we divide both sides of the equation by $7.$

$$
\eqalign{
		7x &= 21 \[5pt]
		\dfrac{7x}{{\color{blue}7}} &=\dfrac{21}{{\color{blue}7}}
	}
$$

 

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $7$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac{7x}{{\color{blue}7}} &=\dfrac{21}{{\color{blue}7}}\[5pt]
		\dfrac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{\color{blue}7}} &=3 \[5pt]
		x &=3
	}
$$

 

Let's check that our answer is correct by plugging it back into the original equation:

$$
\eqalign{
    		7x &=21 \[5pt]
    		7(3) &=21 \[5pt]
		21 &= 21 \; {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
	}
$$

**Note:** If there is a negative coefficient on a variable, we can get rid of it by dividing, like we do with positive coefficients. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y & =10 \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & =\frac{10}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}y}{\cancel{-2}} & =-5 \\ y & =-5\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a74f63d-cfcc-5a3f-899c-6b15cfa2247f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8054 :tutorial/title "Using the Multiplication Principle to Divide"} :step/id #uuid "afb3bda0-823e-547e-bb19-4e9d28f09976" :step/math-academy-id 72112 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055889}} {:db/id 17592186055889 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054837 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054383 :question/id #uuid "68865bc2-e4e2-53d9-9988-4fa962e04746" :question/math-academy-id "e-12861"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e153c18d-6f3e-5fef-a006-c5597cd88bc9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050719}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055033} {:db/id 17592186055274} {:db/id 17592186479844} {:db/id 17592186479891}] :knowledge-point/title "Linear Equations Requiring Division"} :step/id #uuid "1b859cff-8545-5c6f-9fc0-22c30fff2c3b" :step/math-academy-id 72113}] :activity/title "Solving One-Step Multiplication and Division Equations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054901} {:db/id 17592186055883 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056009 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose that we want to solve an equation like

This way, the two negatives will cancel out to form a positive. 

For example, suppose that we have the equation

$$
-x = 3
$$

We can isolate $x$ by multiplying both sides of the equation by $-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =3 \\ (-1)\cdot (-x) & =(-1)\cdot 3 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the equation is $x=-3.$ Let's check to see that this works by substituting our solution back into the original equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =3 \\ -(-3) & =3 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7de479d1-5bb2-5cc9-9fdc-117a02790cab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8053 :tutorial/title "Removing a Negative Sign from a Variable"} :step/id #uuid "91e35f06-1502-52eb-91c6-d755a826ebfc" :step/math-academy-id 72108 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055887}} {:db/id 17592186056010 :tutorial/content "In order to remove a negative sign from our variable, we can multiply both sides by $-1$. In this case, the variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $7.$ To isolate $x$, we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $7$. So, we divide both sides of the equation by $7.$

$$
\eqalign{
		7x &= 21 \[5pt]
		\dfrac{7x}{{\color{blue}7}} &=\dfrac{21}{{\color{blue}7}}
	}
$$

 

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $7$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac{7x}{{\color{blue}7}} &=\dfrac{21}{{\color{blue}7}}\[5pt]
		\dfrac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{\color{blue}7}} &=3 \[5pt]
		x &=3
	}
$$

 

Let's check that our answer is correct by plugging it back into the original equation:

$$
\eqalign{
    		7x &=21 \[5pt]
    		7(3) &=21 \[5pt]
		21 &= 21 \; {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
	}
$$

**Note:** If there is a negative coefficient on a variable, we can get rid of it by dividing, like we do with positive coefficients. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y & =10 \\ \frac{-2y}{-2} & =\frac{10}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}y}{\cancel{-2}} & =-5 \\ y & =-5\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a74f63d-cfcc-5a3f-899c-6b15cfa2247f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8054 :tutorial/title "Using the Multiplication Principle to Divide"} :step/id #uuid "afb3bda0-823e-547e-bb19-4e9d28f09976" :step/math-academy-id 72112 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055889}} {:db/id 17592186056011 :tutorial/content "To solve an equation like $7x = 21$, we again need to look at what's happening to the variable and ask ourselves what the opposite operation is.

Assume that $K>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a square **decreases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to **its side length**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a square* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *inversely proportional its side length*. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{s}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a square is given by 

$$
A={s}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ 2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{2{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2}>0
$$

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{K}{{s}^{2}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373841 :question/id #uuid "20695e23-caba-5b56-9712-3007924a9859" :question/math-academy-id "q-143136"} {:db/id 17592186373848 :question/id #uuid "009d4c8b-f0cf-56da-ae35-04d73a0e9d07" :question/math-academy-id "q-143137"} {:db/id 17592186501189 :question/id #uuid "842c8f8f-382b-5ffe-9458-677d53445332" :question/math-academy-id "q-143130"} {:db/id 17592186501193 :question/id #uuid "8a543fb6-3a0e-5397-9156-31fc05eeae07" :question/math-academy-id "q-143134"} {:db/id 17592186535974 :question/id #uuid "9d65b7da-354a-5fe6-8886-5852de4be621" :question/math-academy-id "q-80488" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5ca4cfd4-07ce-53b0-ac05-7ef895c2e528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{K}{{s}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186535582} {:answer/id #uuid "85d4c3b1-bd0d-5ede-ab88-6b4e89d39b8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=K{s}^{2}" :db/id 17592186535648} {:answer/id #uuid "c0dfbcc4-c509-5a61-956d-8bd3f7248123" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{K}{s}" :db/id 17592186535729} {:answer/id #uuid "c85ccc6a-9e93-5f3b-a97f-d6c05f64a53d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=K" :db/id 17592186535736} {:answer/id #uuid "de7decf8-37f7-5b67-adfa-4152ced74e30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=Ks" :db/id 17592186535777}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186535582} :answer-field/id #uuid "ddc65ecf-2fc0-57a8-93c3-d6c4c4e692c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186535914}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The area of a square increases at a rate that's inversely proportional to its perimeter. *The **area** of a square **increases** at a **rate** that's **inversely proportional** to its **perimeter**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a square* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *increases* at a rate that's *inversely proportional* to its *perimeter.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{4s}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a square is given by 

$$
A={s}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{4s} \\ 2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{4s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{(\frac{k}{4s})}{2s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{8{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{8}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{K}{{s}^{2}}.

Assume that $K>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cube **increases** at a rate that's **inversely proportional** to the **length of its edge**.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cube* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *increases* at a rate that's *inversely proportional to the length of its edge.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k}{s},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cube is given by

$$
V={s}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{s} \\ 3{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{3{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{3}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=\frac{K}{{s}^{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373806 :question/id #uuid "e52629c2-fde8-54a2-9c6a-177590506e80" :question/math-academy-id "q-143126"} {:db/id 17592186373813 :question/id #uuid "ebd4947c-3eb3-5ec1-a356-73f943c86767" :question/math-academy-id "q-143128"} {:db/id 17592186375405 :question/id #uuid "2991e2c6-dc1f-5486-b717-6cc0f03620fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-80487"} {:db/id 17592186501199 :question/id #uuid "9e12d746-15a9-5bf9-9bc2-9113fc7fbbef" :question/math-academy-id "q-38598"} {:db/id 17592186501204 :question/id #uuid "a8090d53-1681-5d0f-a69a-1950471f0a95" :question/math-academy-id "q-66523"} {:db/id 17592186535968 :question/id #uuid "907d5b64-98c1-552d-a43d-a699db06e688" :question/math-academy-id "q-119167" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4eace44a-9542-5986-9bb4-4a121809282b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-k" :db/id 17592186535551} {:answer/id #uuid "5184e724-e665-5cf4-9d18-27d961cdc95d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{r}" :db/id 17592186535561} {:answer/id #uuid "537b4f55-d454-56dc-93a5-b86d06a5d655" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-kr" :db/id 17592186535565} {:answer/id #uuid "71ee97c0-dcb3-5432-b6ad-3f697f647db0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186535609} {:answer/id #uuid "a39bc14a-c886-535c-9199-d7ab15d57b18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2}" :db/id 17592186535689}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186535551} :answer-field/id #uuid "13b9af92-d428-5ecd-80c2-21192da8e8da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186535837}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The volume of a sphere decreases at a rate that's proportional to its surface area. Assume that $k>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*Its **volume decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to its **surface area**.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to its surface area $S.$* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kS,
$$

where $k>0.$ Now, using the fact that $S=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-4\pi k{r}^{2}.
$$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi k{r}^{2} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{4\pi k{r}^{2}}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188292 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187996 :question/id #uuid "b657adbb-c3c4-54c2-8c2c-44ccc0bf9c3a" :question/math-academy-id "e-10076"} :knowledge-point/id What differential equation describes this curve?" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **distance from $P$ to the origin**.*

We note the following:

- The *distance from $P(x,y)$ to the origin* is given by $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional* to the distance from $P$ to the origin, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}=k\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}=k\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188916 :question/id #uuid "a41dc2f9-6f09-555a-8599-d1ec0edb3723" :question/math-academy-id "q-38563"} {:db/id 17592186373792 :question/id #uuid The derivative at the point $(3,-5)$ equals $24.$ What differential equation describes this curve?" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional to* the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot |x|
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k|x|.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=24$ when at the point $(3,-5).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}24=k|3|\,⟹\,k=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=8|x|.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373869 :question/id #uuid "6313157a-186a-55a3-bc68-314f95023aa8" :question/math-academy-id "q-143141"} {:db/id 17592186373876 :question/id #uuid 17592186189107}} {:db/id 17592186189104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189375 :tutorial/content "When constructing a differential equation to model a particular phenomenon, we sometimes combine several pieces of information to create the correct model.

Consider the following situation:

*The common cold virus spreads through a particular country. The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t$ (in days) since the outbreak started. 
Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**.*

We want to find a differential equation that models $P(t),$ the number of infected people. We note the following:

- The statement describes the *rate* at which the *number of infected people* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t.$ Therefore, if $I(t)$ represents the rate at which infections increase, then

$$
I(t) = kt^2,
$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

- Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**. Therefore, if $D(t)$ represents the rate at which infections decrease, then

$$
D(t) = 100.
$$

Therefore, the differential equation that describes this phenomenon is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t} & ={{k{t}^{2}-100}_{⏟}}_{I(t)-D(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Although we introduced the functions $I(t)$ and $D(t)$ here, we can usually write down the appropriate differential equation straight away. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a7ad3b5-e4de-56c0-8fc9-8a9b2c976094" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "37206e3d-9800-567e-82f6-eed74a977f1f" Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the side length, $s(t),$ in this process. Assume that $K>0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a square **decreases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to **its side length**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a square* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *inversely proportional its side length*. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{s}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a square is given by 

$$
A={s}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ 2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{s} \\ \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{2{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2}>0
$$

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{K}{{s}^{2}}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "17e24c4d-fbe4-5267-b369-1dc13301b94c"} {:db/id 17592186536021 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188915 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00359f0d-5c3b-50c1-a12e-737bc41221da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{′}(x)=k({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})" :db/id 17592186535436} {:answer/id #uuid "3c96294f-e5cd-511a-981b-9f5670bd9a23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{′}(x)=k{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186535527} {:answer/id #uuid "7e897ffd-840e-5b35-92d6-f6d2bd060f6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{′}(x)=k\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186535635} {:answer/id #uuid "ec89e486-9020-5137-9ccb-884bab47d61f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{′}(x)=k{x}^{2}{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186535800} {:answer/id #uuid "f7ffbb76-ca6f-595c-aa26-024793132497" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{y}^{′}(x)=kxy" :db/id 17592186535813}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186535635} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ce498ff-bed5-5a31-b8d4-a763ddd397a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186187566}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5deb4667-ba88-546b-92cb-11999248cbcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-38329" :question/problem "At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ is proportional to the distance from $P$ to the origin. What differential equation describes this curve?" :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **distance from $P$ to the origin**.*

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({s}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2s\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$
