the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse"}] :question/problem "Find the minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=16x_1^2+16x_1x_2+x_2^2$ given that $16x_1^2 + x_2^2=16,$ and find the vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the minimum is obtained." :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:
![](images/ef/ef4c1994a6c3980934ab8b95a92be32293c434fa84a0ffb70dc82cf3198367b2.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x_1^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{4^2}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=4$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1={x_1} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{4},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 
![](images/df/dfa724469e02e9851ec5dc895fe7dda810836745d3a1781a8c60f01d09fbd32b.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}= Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 & 8 \\ 8 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 8 \\ 32 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimise $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}16-\lambda  & 32 \\ 32 & 16-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )(16-\lambda )-1\,024 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-32\lambda -768 & =0 \\ (\lambda -48)(\lambda +16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =48,\,-16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\min \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{min}} = -16.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}=-16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-16I) & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{bmatrix}+16\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}32 & 32 \\ 32 & 32\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-16I))\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/49/49d16ecc1b8c785d665bd961f24f5627f18fceec2a74dee5b2b1f4c39f2864a8.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](images/18/18d7c92aca6dc096a79cf0ae8ea6ef99e058da58481689af353f430e726b69a5.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048300} {:db/id 17592186049456} {:db/id 17592186198684 :question/id #uuid "38171cb4-52a5-5ebe-b692-159c5b30da34" :question/math-academy-id "q-170138" :knowledge-point/_questions :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $40.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -6 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $40,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=40.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=40:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-40I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{bmatrix}-40\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-36 & -12 \\ -12 & -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-40I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$

$$

$$

$$

$x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198444 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389855 :question/id #uuid "9517d41a-5a17-54a5-b8d2-6ea1cb7908a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-179407"} {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186492837 :question/id #uuid "1e463920-832a-54ce-b343-95505e40d97a" :question/math-academy-id "q-170527" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c4c2ff5-edba-514a-87a6-58daf1e367d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492271} {:answer/id #uuid "5b0214e5-26b9-58f4-866b-8bc611fb2ef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492397} {:answer/id #uuid "d70b4dc0-8536-581a-8bd5-450e119abdcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492642} {:answer/id #uuid "eb3d2221-dc50-598c-ba5a-1cb5379b5184" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492672} {:answer/id #uuid "f99577b0-7bae-5456-97fc-603ae4a89241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492696}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186492642} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4ec5a8e-4792-5032-a904-759d0e616ab6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186492779}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9,$ is $-18.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$

$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

$$

45752 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199396}} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/a6/a6165f41eb43e8f6e8fd4399f1c428f73481de9d4b5ec41293f3ec0e4f062fc6.svg)

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/30/30699c4f0abcb099a6f7a76cbd76674757c3f7de313e034d0870d1fce27fdd8c.svg)

{:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} :step/id #uuid "f3b4db0d-8fec-573f-8597-7e9b0d0a4474" :step/math-academy-id 45758 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199395}} {:db/id 17592186199404 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038}] :activity/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms: Determining Where Extrema are Attained" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198510} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:

\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038} {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} {:db/id 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$

$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046658} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186502197} :activity/id #uuid $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "592400bd-60ae-541a-a9a4-3378b493d7a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186502174}} {:db/id 17592186502174 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284645 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58e43fd8-bedb-54d5-9723-4873762018ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186282444} {:answer/id #uuid "6080b967-b1e5-508e-9eb9-b06f08ffc56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186282507} {:answer/id #uuid "b44dda1b-d74d-5302-ac25-2322f81791f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186283250} {:answer/id #uuid "f9c243a3-3d78-5363-a946-67271923a982" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186283874} {:answer/id #uuid "fdac630b-fc7e-5910-8320-fe5c826d997e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186283913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282444} :answer-field/id #uuid "b28de760-832c-5bd3-997a-40bc410c2fcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284244}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "315ff370-acb2-54c0-a94c-7932c53e50d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170525" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7b55ab94-44ca-5e5f-8316-aab35be9951d"} {:db/id 17592186514542 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$

$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7b55ab94-44ca-5e5f-8316-aab35be9951d"} {:db/id 17592186514542 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-18,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-18.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-18:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-18)I & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}+18\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}36 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-18)I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "491341df-0c55-56c0-a053-5047b84d6caf"} {:db/id 17592186519649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198685 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "964ff685-0c8f-5399-a6db-e7e9ff284b45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-80" :db/id 17592186194742} {:answer/id #uuid "c4372638-eac2-5651-a42e-b474aa8e5014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-160" :db/id 17592186194743} {:answer/id #uuid "e585951e-1933-5d5a-a55e-f897fdd4664a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-100" :db/id 17592186194744} {:answer/id #uuid "135fadcd-1711-57c3-92f2-65d7240f6b44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-40" :db/id 17592186194745} {:answer/id #uuid "5642d232-0433-5476-bf0e-5697fbc0a389" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-140" :db/id 17592186194746}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186194746} :answer-field/id #uuid "223a3270-62e6-5297-b31c-f1bd2215a506" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186194741}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8a89d201-6c7f-5b6a-9c34-e445b93c0f7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-170160" :question/problem "Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=5{x}_{1}^{2}-16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $25{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=5$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -16 \\ -40 & -20\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -80 \\ -80 & -100\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}20-\lambda  & -80 \\ -80 & -100-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (20-\lambda )(-100-\lambda )-6\,400 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+80\lambda -8\,400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -60)(\lambda +140) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =60,\,-140\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-140.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8d69128b-9c71-5aba-b4db-fd173418e1a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519657}} {:db/id 17592186519632 :step/content {:db/id 17592186492837 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c4c2ff5-edba-514a-87a6-58daf1e367d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492271} {:answer/id #uuid "5b0214e5-26b9-58f4-866b-8bc611fb2ef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492397} {:answer/id #uuid "d70b4dc0-8536-581a-8bd5-450e119abdcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492642} {:answer/id #uuid "eb3d2221-dc50-598c-ba5a-1cb5379b5184" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492672} {:answer/id #uuid "f99577b0-7bae-5456-97fc-603ae4a89241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186492696}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186492642} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4ec5a8e-4792-5032-a904-759d0e616ab6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186492779}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1e463920-832a-54ce-b343-95505e40d97a" :question/math-academy-id "q-170527" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9,$ is $-18.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-18,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-18.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-18:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-18)I & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}+18\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}36 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-18)I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "491341df-0c55-56c0-a053-5047b84d6caf"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c4c2ff5-edba-514a-87a6-58daf1e367d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value
