:db/id 17592186228132}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ -3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186229682 :question/id #uuid "62010a37-a91d-55bc-8c8e-6361d12d6c44" :question/math-academy-id "q-335267" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "77290e62-6148-5a0c-a377-bec8579eec5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186309679} {:answer/id #uuid "97fc3697-404e-5fb0-854e-fc0c8ff7d45c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-3t} \\ 2t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186309968} {:answer/id #uuid "9a02425e-0f01-5418-94f2-288ad58f1b27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186309988} {:answer/id #uuid "a7c51a8a-3c2a-5bdb-a554-d4a1fb8e8ca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ -2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186310100} {:answer/id #uuid "d266e8d7-9b0b-5943-9acc-ac02de0e98d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186310440}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186310440} :answer-field/id #uuid "a01f0c87-7802-5bf3-a753-2547be1ae761" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186311255}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-3y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308537 :question/id #uuid "b59372b5-46f1-5738-9ccc-9025ae0786e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-333971"} {:db/id 17592186311559 :question/id #uuid "622243a2-b3f9-5f58-9668-ac4d025f3264" :question/math-academy-id "q-335260" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4386227a-d159-5ea7-b586-57eb8ba8b3dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{sin}(5t)+\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186309258} {:answer/id #uuid "ce0f7ff2-63f3-536e-a712-0b2b5f23cf38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sin(5t)+\cos(5t)" :db/id 17592186506276}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506276} :answer-field/id #uuid "53651861-1195-570e-a314-53031aadafea" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311008} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17eab3e0-25a6-5d97-ab26-3bfb684afa0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}(5t)-3\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186308938} {:answer/id #uuid "2633b2d1-98e4-54f9-bd3d-9d6754122e46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\cos(5t)+\sin(5t)" :db/id 17592186505974}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505974} :answer-field/id #uuid "d170c52a-07fe-5c77-8bee-10ab3fcdbfb2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311400}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

$$

$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ is true by $\text{the properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the

{{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$"} {:db/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by

- We first consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L6}$, and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

Using $\text{L6}$, we substitute $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})$ to obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L6}$ by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can combine the exponentials:

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7}$ gives line $\text{L8}.$ Thus, line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{the fact [{:db/id 17592186230002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "978fc2f4-910c-5bef-9ae3-3da9377642ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14515 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c774d65b-c500-58e4-aa9a-e222d3d136ae" :step/math-academy-id 592270 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230003}} {:db/id 17592186230003 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229142 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228910 :question/id #uuid "26df399d-cd87-5b5d-9f3f-7ced4ca5fd06" :question/math-academy-id "e-21707"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5bc609b-dc5b-52e9-9f0e-206f32bb829b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050125} {:db/id 17592186050228}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229669} {:db/id 17592186229677} {:db/id 17592186308684} {:db/id 17592186308685} {:db/id 17592186402113} {:db/id 17592186445608} {:db/id 17592186445610} {:db/id 17592186445613}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "d3b52974-38d7-50fa-b648-b51510a9a617" :step/math-academy-id 592271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230004}} {:db/id 17592186230004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230193 :tutorial/content "Now, let's find the solution to the initial value problem below

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/5c/5c4ed0a2e9db0979e4fc0342c2e4db7c23c60cf58293a496fa661ff1c03fccde.svg)
where ![](images/71/7164659247c5290544655b05943d7d998f67cb1cc3b4cc45bab0902e8059bc75.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/e3/e3f94e8ce2cc2063d469fbac2af87232cc130f788243c1507bfe9972dd4b04c1.svg)

Recall that the general solution of the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Evaluating both sides of $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{c}$ at $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & ={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c \\ x(0) & ={e}^{A(0)}\,c \\ x(0) & =I\,c \\ c & =x(0).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to our initial value problem is 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0).
$$

Computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/fc/fc4e1ba16be420fbe5e53e2dbb4ee6da96c7097bbe4e117315407ec4dc65365f.svg)

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{7t} & t{e}^{7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(3-2t){e}^{7t} \\ -2{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9cb11887-9535-5a54-a180-eb20a7534696" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14529 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems"} :step/id #uuid "5206e604-fe74-5b8a-800c-cdb747dc1e28" :step/math-academy-id 592274 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230005}} {:db/id 17592186230005 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229143 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228918 :question/id #uuid "ead811e0-8551-5b15-8b49-711cbe0b8498" :question/math-academy-id "e-21725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d611c75-818f-508f-a7a4-49edb32baa41" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229657} {:db/id 17592186229682} {:db/id 17592186308537} {:db/id 17592186311559} {:db/id 17592186311560} {:db/id 17592186311561} {:db/id 17592186311562} {:db/id 17592186311563} {:db/id 17592186372698} {:db/id 17592186372703} {:db/id 17592186445609} {:db/id 17592186445611} {:db/id 17592186482598}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "c93fbf09-3c42-5a66-8e76-1cf0d810f44a" :step/math-academy-id 592275 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230006}} {:db/id 17592186230006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230194 :tutorial/content "Next, let's find the solution to the initial value problem

given that ![](images/ee/ee25228bf71d1b7d9d0688af06a7f1335c252310127b403ed0ed37f7fe277c07.svg) where ![](images/3a/3a3ac9326741c0e2390a8e2f079808f0b432b740149ef4b034ffa7568dc33848.svg)

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/2b/2b81cf358ffb3df49f327b63138640ac452a249f989353b521be34d531aeffd9.svg)
where ![](images/11/1110f0bdbe784b21683bfb9610ca9c04e5a45755954d49a15124e530feef2002.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/47/47d8a0214e5ccdf6625a330d23003dec11cbc3a4f35cb2992df29a688963e4b2.svg)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}.$ We can determine the constant vector $\mathbf{c}$ using the initial condition at time $t=t_0{:}$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \implies \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

since the inverse of $e^{At_0}$ is $e^{-At_0}.$ Plugging this back into our general solution gives the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our specific problem (with $t_0=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fe9a975-9d92-5f79-8a67-34af55196fb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14530 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems With Shifted Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "19b34f7c-755c-5e1b-a16f-22bd17d1ecc7" :step/math-academy-id 592278 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230007}} {:db/id 17592186230007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229144 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228917 :question/id #uuid "b061f2b1-b015-582f-921f-9b444db631ee" :question/math-academy-id "e-21723"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37e58bb6-6d90-5171-bba2-6ffa5a0c91d9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229664} {:db/id 17592186229684} {:db/id 17592186311564} {:db/id 17592186311590} {:db/id 17592186311591} {:db/id 17592186311592} {:db/id 17592186311593} {:db/id 17592186311594} {:db/id 17592186391579} {:db/id 17592186391586} {:db/id 17592186445615} {:db/id 17592186482582} {:db/id 17592186535011}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "633a401e-5116-5c9e-a0b4-8848cf596d7b" :step/math-academy-id 592279 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230008}} {:db/id 17592186230008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "978fc2f4-910c-5bef-9ae3-3da9377642ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14515 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c774d65b-c500-58e4-aa9a-e222d3d136ae" :step/math-academy-id 592270 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230003}} {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ae3cfa7-a5a5-5a50-aefa-8b8dec561567" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14528 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Properties of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "eb56047e-3845-5f8e-9282-d41f308270e3" :step/math-academy-id 592282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230009}} {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=9y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=9x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 9 \\ 9 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(9t) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(9t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2379b8ac-5990-5a88-876d-7a3b13ce4148" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482645}} {:db/id 17592186482629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186482509 :question/answer-fields Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-3)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-3))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-3)) \\ -2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-3))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c1447d08-16ad-539a-8ebf-f17fc52a738b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482629}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "59d8cb4f-ee06-5141-9f71-0005f275d41d" :answer/type {:db/id $$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\, \\ \,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-3x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(-1) \\ y(-1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-(-1))}\,x(-1) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "27866c4a-22d7-5b58-972c-cfe8b9d40b47" :step/next {:db/id 17592186506617}} {:db/id 17592186506615 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311559 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4386227a-d159-5ea7-b586-57eb8ba8b3dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{sin}(5t)+\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186309258} {:answer/id #uuid "ce0f7ff2-63f3-536e-a712-0b2b5f23cf38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sin(5t)+\cos(5t)" :db/id 17592186506276}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506276} :answer-field/id #uuid "53651861-1195-570e-a314-53031aadafea" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311008} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17eab3e0-25a6-5d97-ab26-3bfb684afa0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}(5t)-3\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186308938} {:answer/id #uuid "2633b2d1-98e4-54f9-bd3d-9d6754122e46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\cos(5t)+\sin(5t)" :db/id 17592186505974}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505974} :answer-field/id #uuid "d170c52a-07fe-5c77-8bee-10ab3fcdbfb2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311400}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "622243a2-b3f9-5f58-9668-ac4d025f3264" :question/math-academy-id "q-335260" :question/problem "$$

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "45874040-9e7b-5fb5-9a00-ef344d9b3cd1" :question/math-academy-id "q-337109" :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$  Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$  Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$"} :step/id #uuid "323902b1-2dc9-5b75-a6de-c749bb49c955"} $$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ is true by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, every solution of the system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ is true by $\text{the properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$"} :step/id #uuid "94ec5f0a-352f-5ac0-bc02-f9deb9d28d5c"} $$

To solve the compound inequality, we apply the usual operations to the middle of the inequality to isolate $x.$ Keep in mind that whatever we do to the middle, we also need to do to *both* the left-hand *and* right-hand sides.

Here, we can isolate $x$ by subtracting $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	4 & \le x + 2 \le 8 \[5pt]
	4 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} &\le x + 2 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \le 8 \,{\color{red}-}\, {\color{red}{2}} \[5pt]
	2 &\le x \le 6
}
$$

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{m},{y}_{m}) & =(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2}) \\ (1,4) & =(\frac{-5+a}{2},\frac{3+b}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding $x$- and $y$-coordinates in the equation above gives us

$$

[{:db/id 17592186074600 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075050 :tutorial/content "In the coordinate plane, the **midpoint** of a line segment with endpoints $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ lies halfway between the $x$-coordinates $x_1$ and $x_2$, and halfway between the $y$-coordinates $y_1$ and $y_2$.

The coordinates of the midpoint can be computed using the formula

$$
(x_m,y_m) = \left(\dfrac{x_1 +x_2}2,\dfrac{y_1+y_2}2\right)
$$

For example, the coordinates of the midpoint of a line segment with endpoints $(2,1)$ and $(6,13)$ can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x_{m}, y_{m}) &= (\frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2}, \frac{y_{1} + y_{2}}{2}) \\
&= (\frac{2 + 6}{2}, \frac{1 + 13}{2}) \\
&= (\frac{8}{2}, \frac{14}{2}) \\
&= (4, 7)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "164a0bd6-c234-5906-82c5-f00aefe19504" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8897 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "eecc366e-853e-52a8-bc68-b16fc245ecce" :step/math-academy-id 154975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074601}} {:db/id 17592186074601 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073713 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073483 :question/id #uuid "68fc6ab1-0c7b-50b2-b541-137be5f5572e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "92c49ea0-7ec5-5ffc-8a36-c4f46f78fda7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050476} {:db/id 17592186050517}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074065} {:db/id 17592186074170} {:db/id 17592186233438} {:db/id 17592186233493} {:db/id 17592186233630}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Midpoint of a Segment"} :step/id #uuid "ee2327aa-02a2-5e9b-b07c-07c22671f4fc" :step/math-academy-id 154976 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074602}} {:db/id 17592186074602 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073714 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073484 :question/id #uuid "ca03fd37-a09e-5546-95a5-12f0cd1657c6" :question/math-academy-id "e-14358"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "58e2e40e-209b-5bc7-98df-11841c2bbcc3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074019} {:db/id 17592186074066} {:db/id 17592186074071} {:db/id 17592186233202} {:db/id 17592186233637} {:db/id 17592186233638} {:db/id 17592186233639} {:db/id 17592186234357} {:db/id 17592186290348} {:db/id 17592186290349} {:db/id 17592186290350} {:db/id 17592186342069}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Midpoint of a Segment With Variable Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "a966a4b4-4e42-5a47-812c-3a495619e03c" :step/math-academy-id 154979 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074603}} {:db/id 17592186074603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075051 :tutorial/content "Suppose $M(4,2)$ is the midpoint between $A(1,1)$ and $B(a,b)$. \begin{aligned}
(x_{m}, y_{m}) &= (\frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2}, \frac{y_{1} + y_{2}}{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} &= 1, & y_{1}|= 1, \\ x_{2}|= a, & y_{2}|= b, \\ x_{m}|= 4, & y_{m}|= 2\end{bmatrix}

$$

$$
{4 = \frac{1 + a}{2}; 2 = \frac{1 + b}{2}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equations by $2$, we have:

$$
{8 = 1 + a; 4 = 1 + b
$$

Finally, we solve both equations independently:

$$
{a = 8 - 1 = 7; b = 4 - 1 = 3
$$

$$

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left(3^{x}\right)
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+1 = x \log_2 \left(3\right)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x{log}_{2}⁡(3)-x & =1 \\ x({log}_{2}⁡(3)-1) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{2}⁡(3)-1}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{y}={4}^{y+1} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{y}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =y{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y-y{log}_{5}⁡4 & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y(1-{log}_{5}⁡4) & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{5}⁡4}{1-{log}_{5}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(4)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.861\,353.
$$

Finally, then, we can approximate $y$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}y≈\frac{0.861\,353}{1-0.861\,353}≈6.213,\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3737} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180666 :tutorial/content "The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation. 
For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

### General Case

In general, let's consider an equation of the form

\[
a^{f(x)} = b^{g(x)},
\]

where [math]a[/math] and [math]b[/math] are different constants that can't be presented as powers of the same base, and [math]f(x)[/math], [math]g(x)[/math] are some functions.
We now can apply 
\[
\log_a
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\log_b
\]
as well as the common logarithm ([math]\log[/math]) or the natural logarithm ([math]\ln[/math]) on both sides of our equation to get rid of the exponents." :tutorial/id #uuid can use the quotient rule for radicals, which states 

$$
\dfrac {\sqrt {a}} {\sqrt{b}} = \sqrt{\dfrac a b}.
$$

For example, let's simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{16w^2}{25}}$

First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\dfrac{16w^2}{25}}  = \dfrac {\sqrt{16w^2}} {\color{blue}\sqrt{25}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{16w^2}}{\color{blue}\sqrt{5^2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{16w^2}}{\color{blue}5}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression under the radical as a perfect square and taking its square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{16{w}^{2}}}{5} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{(4w)^{2}}}{5} & = \\ \frac{|4w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{|4|\cdot |w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{4\cdot |w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{4|w|}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7bfc07d9-feb0-5bcc-b3f0-50bb42eb2b6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6691 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2bc45b7b-b768-5e67-92eb-6d8dfdb26080" :step/math-academy-id 40513 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069777}} {:db/id 17592186069777 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068836 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068442 :question/id #uuid "dd7c79e5-d274-5f04-af44-335b5a6d95df" :question/math-academy-id "e-10699"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bc723e84-3051-5e73-ac57-08da7193c368" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050315} {:db/id 17592186050496}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069096} {:db/id 17592186069423} {:db/id 17592186503656} {:db/id 17592186503672}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Radical Expressions With Perfect Squares Under the Radical"} :step/id #uuid "92bbfce1-1705-5e28-a0bf-e544d5fecdf9" :step/math-academy-id 40520 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069780}} {:db/id 17592186069778 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069999 :tutorial/content "The quotient rule for radicals also works for higher-order roots, like the cube root:

$$

$$

In general, we have the following result:

$$
\sqrt[n]{ \dfrac a b } = \dfrac{ \sqrt[n]{a} }{ \sqrt[n]{b} }

Unit Sphere"}] :question/problem "A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are $7, 2,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 7
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\}  = \sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$"} {:db/id 17592186048432} {:db/id 17592186162360 :question/id #uuid "b2e59ffd-322c-5739-bff6-4abbfbcffef1" :question/math-academy-id "q-139415" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5884f354-e5d3-5445-b252-6177d7fb10d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186266935} {:answer/id #uuid "59a2b792-bce2-5ab3-8129-3ed501c97fa1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186266941} {:answer/id #uuid "66a53c17-6cca-59e9-b3a7-10509d1e6f05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267055} {:answer/id #uuid "7ed785dc-de4a-56df-9005-91dc3382836b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186267261} {:answer/id #uuid "c268b638-dc68-5720-86dc-4bdf86ac9c78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186267877}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266941} :answer-field/id #uuid "71f2e673-2942-5733-b153-c9e00dd002b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268619}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=7\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$"} {:db/id 17592186269230 :question/id #uuid "e48008ac-4acd-5d33-8b94-d523fa814086" :question/math-academy-id "q-139492" Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form"}] :question/problem "![](images/09/094b6043b9cce7f3ac2a7cc32fa53785d3fbf5b490ce853474f89bb4afa8291a.png)

A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ are unit eigenvectors of $A^TA,$ find an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of $A^T A?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A^T A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n.
$$

Then,

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

- $\cdots$

In our example, we see that

- $||A\mathbf v_1|| = 8 = \sigma_1,$ which means that $\lambda_1 = 8^2 = 64,$ and

- $||A\mathbf v_2|| = 6 = \sigma_2,$ which means that $\lambda_2 = 6^2 = 36.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 36$ of $A^T A$ is $\mathbf{v}_2.$"} {:db/id 17592186162362 :question/id #uuid "ba175b74-8169-5d32-9cc8-7cf8e202ba3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-139420"} {:db/id 17592186162363 :question/id #uuid "14414eae-18ed-5455-a3d4-1f9724606970" :question/math-academy-id "q-139421" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27612a52-9a44-5194-990a-b67bd5b0cb3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{1}" :db/id 17592186266495} {:answer/id #uuid "3781afe7-ca23-5caf-8d77-e210ce87765d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186266623} {:answer/id #uuid "9cbfef3a-23de-5494-b267-533971519fee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267552} {:answer/id #uuid "a48b2a55-e19f-5a3b-aad5-9311f9e9ad3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{2}" :db/id 17592186267628} {:answer/id #uuid "a9e9b4e6-ef6f-5008-83b9-4dc476b26261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7{v}_{1}+5{v}_{2}" :db/id 17592186267677}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267628} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f73eb28-9edf-5454-bbc8-1e8090f60bd5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268549}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/f2/f26e876d5234313926a2cbaa8938e32c8a725cf3435ce3113361bfa3dc1b7997.png)

Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $25$ of ${A}^{T}A?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

\big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$"} {:db/id 17592186162361 :question/id #uuid "cdd91aaf-b8dd-5936-93a2-ee3b24ba20f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-139418" $$

$$

$$

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={8}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=8.
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= -x^{2} + 2x + 6 \\
&= - (x^{2} - 2x) + 6 \\
&= - (x^{2} - 2 \cdot x + 1^{2} - 1^{2}) + 6 \\
&= - ((x - 1)^{2} - 1) + 6 \\
&= - (x - 1)^{2} + 1 + 6 \\
&= - (x - 1)^{2} + 7
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$.

$$
y = -(x-1)^2+ 7
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$.

$$
x = -(y-1)^2+ 7
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= - (y - 1)^{2} + 7 \\
x - 7 &= - (y - 1)^{2} \\
7 - x &= (y - 1)^{2} \\
\sqrt{7 - x} &= y - 1 \\
\sqrt{7 - x} + 1 &= y
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we selected the positive square root because if the domain of $f(x)$ is

$$
x \geq 1
$$

then the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
f^{-1} \geq 1
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$.

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{7-x} +1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051078} {:db/id 17592186184551 :question/id #uuid "bca5ae99-6b07-51d2-9c2a-96dd3f7f4271" :question/math-academy-id "q-220372"} {:db/id 17592186184791 :question/id #uuid "4bdd04d6-43b2-524d-bc2d-75ca4990de22" :question/math-academy-id "q-46408"} {:db/id 17592186184166 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186183954 :question/id #uuid "836ac184-e55d-5c32-a4af-8a0da847a423" :question/math-academy-id "e-14879"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "02655639-b390-510d-9eda-3221375e7e5e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184552 :question/id #uuid "629de3ed-ef46-5ff0-bd91-8c4fa7e9f037" :question/math-academy-id "q-220374"} {:db/id 17592186184789 :question/id #uuid "e2e323d3-460f-5bcb-be71-a754f4dd2852" :question/math-academy-id "q-46347"}] :knowledge-point/title "The Negative Square Root Case"} {:db/id 17592186183954 :question/id #uuid "836ac184-e55d-5c32-a4af-8a0da847a423" :question/math-academy-id "e-14879" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186184166 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "02655639-b390-510d-9eda-3221375e7e5e" :knowledge-point/title "The Negative Square Root Case"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 2$ for $x \leq 3$." :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

So, to calculate the inverse of a quadratic function, we must first restrict its domain.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic function:

$$
f(x)=(x-2)^2-3
$$

Since the function is in vertex form, we can immediately see that the vertex of the corresponding parabola $y=f(x)$ is located at $(2,-3)$. Therefore, the function $f(x)$ will be one-to-one if we restrict its domain to either

$$
x\leq 2
$$

or

$$
x\geq 2
$$

Let's restrict the domain to

$$
x\geq 2
$$

The graph of $y=f(x)$ for

$$
x\geq 2
$$

is shown below.

![](images/05/059fc0ffddc4b590de8597d3252a6901c7da16063e16b2b4a9a7b24383ce83f7.png)

Now that $f(x)$ is one-to-one, we can calculate its inverse. We follow the four usual steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$.

$$
y = (x-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$.

$$
x = (y-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (y - 2)^{2} - 3 \\
x + 3 &= (y - 2)^{2} \\
\sqrt{x + 3} &= y - 2 \\
\sqrt{x + 3} + 2 &= y
\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The *domain* of the original function is the *range* of the inverse function. In our case, since the domain of $f$ is

$$
x \geq 2
$$

the range of the inverse must be

$$
f^{-1} \geq 2
$$

Therefore, we select the positive square root in the third step above. Indeed, notice that

$$
\sqrt{x + 3} +2 \geq 2
$$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$.

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x + 3} +2
$$

We're done!" :tutorial/id #uuid "783dd423-f37c-5794-a3be-b018f146724c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9258 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c88a3ac6-6ff0-5d00-811e-a83529593d3d" The diagram above shows a unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $-0.7$, what is the value of $\cos\theta$?" :question/worked-solution "Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta
$$

![](images/f4/f438a90ea7afe511562058f49f13af29722aa137a8032a22ac16ca6566688cb7.png)

We're given that $x=-0.7$ at the point $P$. Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = -0.7
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050291} {:db/id 17592186060327 :question/id #uuid "e8ae7019-4c0d-54fc-ac24-d9e53ebc4b9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-64575"} {:db/id 17592186060328 :question/id #uuid "2413797a-e1e5-5a18-8246-5d3a02ebead6" :question/math-academy-id "q-64580"} {:db/id 17592186059831 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059390 :question/id #uuid "ea7f4d67-8d88-559f-b39e-7618d86f9379" :question/math-academy-id "e-10819"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "41b43c0b-f0bb-54eb-9644-6db9398ab0a9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050795}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060074 :question/id #uuid "b0cef338-42f6-5b2f-86eb-627321869565" :question/math-academy-id "q-1587"} {:db/id 17592186060075 :question/id #uuid "5012c763-b9bc-59ff-b006-c570dcca7dae" :question/math-academy-id "q-1590"}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Sine of an Angle in Terms of a Reference Angle"} {:db/id 17592186059390 :question/id #uuid "ea7f4d67-8d88-559f-b39e-7618d86f9379" :question/math-academy-id "e-10819" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059831 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "41b43c0b-f0bb-54eb-9644-6db9398ab0a9" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Sine of an Angle in Terms of a Reference Angle"}] :question/problem "What is $\sin 335^\circ$ expressed in terms of a reference angle?" :question/worked-solution "To express $\sin{335^\circ}$ in terms of $\sin\theta_R$, we follow three steps:

1. Find its reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the function for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

First, let's draw the angle $335^\circ$ in the coordinate plane (CAST diagram):

![](images/a7/a7456b0617c3c03ad55403e58904be26d826c90611c1a323553fa5c9f3149d66.png)

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = 335^\circ
$$

is in the $4$th quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= 360^{∘} - θ \\
&= 360^{∘} - 335^{∘} \\
&= 25^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\sin{335^\circ}$, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\sin\theta_R = \sin{25^\circ}
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\sin{335^\circ}$ must be *negative* because the sine ratio is *always* negative in the $4$th quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin 335^\circ = -\sin{25^\circ}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060074 :question/id #uuid "b0cef338-42f6-5b2f-86eb-627321869565" :question/math-academy-id "q-1587" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059831 :knowledge-point/id #uuid of a reference angle?" :question/worked-solution "To express $\cos{340^\circ}$ in terms of $\cos\theta_R$, we follow three steps:

1. Find its reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the function for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

First, let's draw the angle $340^\circ$ in the coordinate plane (CAST diagram):

![](images/c2/c263e4358de9cd29f1a97795e840d06cf4b198cf53c0630c2c12c85de7f00490.png)

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = 340^\circ
$$

is in the $4$th quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= 360^{∘} - θ \\
&= 360^{∘} - 340^{∘} \\
&= 20^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\cos{340^\circ}$, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\cos\theta_R = \cos{20^\circ}
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\cos{340^\circ}$ must be *positive* because the cosine ratio is *always* positive in the $4$th quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\cos 340^\circ = \cos{20^\circ}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060329 :question/id #uuid "7f4f7b8b-fc7f-5b1e-bb19-2746ee23424b" :question/math-academy-id "q-64634" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059832 :knowledge-point/id #uuid &= 180^{∘} - 162^{∘} \\

\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\tan{162^\circ}$, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\tan\theta_R = \tan{18^\circ}
$$

$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060739 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060861 :tutorial/content "We can use reference angles to evaluate trigonometric ratios for angles outside the first quadrant.

To demonstrate, let's determine the value of $\cos (135^\circ)$, corresponding to the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the unit circle, as shown below.

![](images/be/bef50a070785e4bb86867ba6404942fd7eaa04b60720adfb04176bafe2fa2121.png)

The reference angle for

$$
\theta=135^\circ
$$

is

$$
\theta_R=45^\circ
$$

Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/33/33b208e44aaa556a67ebaf7a6c1117b09adf863c56deb1bc1f5590e289062c4b.png)

Let $P'$ be the image of $P$ under a reflection across the $y$-axis. This gives a pair of congruent angles of measure $45^\circ$, as shown.

![](images/c4/c4875682498edaadc74a8af238fdf3293b4820025256df78e60867940061785e.png)

According to the definition, $\cos(135^\circ)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$. But this is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point $P'$ *taken with the opposite sign.*

The $x$-coordinate of $P'$ equals the cosine of the reference angle.

$$
\cos(45^\circ)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\cos(\, \underbrace{135^\circ}_{\theta} \,) =-\cos(\, \underbrace{45^\circ}_{\theta_R} \,) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

So, we simplified the evaluation of $\cos(135^\circ)$ by evaluating the cosine of the corresponding reference angle

$$
\theta_R=45^\circ
$$

*with an additional sign adjustment* for the final result.

We can use a similar argument to show that, since

$$
y = \sin\theta
$$

we have

$$
\sin(135^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}
$$

In this case, we do **NOT** change the sign because the $y$-coordinates of $P'$ and $P$ *are equal.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "8c1461a2-d5b4-5d11-b0ad-6537ca726992" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10532 :tutorial/title "Calculating Trigonometric Ratios Using Reference Angles"} :step/id #uuid "bdeb7825-3a44-52de-9875-55a1ffbcd7e7" :step/math-academy-id 210844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060778}} {:db/id 17592186060776 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060971 :tutorial/content "As we've seen, the cosine and sine ratios for *acute* angles can be defined in the following ways:

- Using a right triangle. If $\theta$ is an acute angle in a right triangle, then
$\cos\theta = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}$.
- Using the unit circle. If $\theta$ is a central angle made by a point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle in the first quadrant, then
$\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y$.

We can't define trigonometric ratios for non-acute angles using right triangles because a right triangle can't have angles larger than $90^\circ$. However, we can *extend* these ratios for non-acute angles using unit circles.

To do that, let's consider the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ in any quadrant, measured in the usual way.

![](images/61/612d468ea23fefb6bbb33bd676a1930604b283475f36be08541419776bb580bd.png)

We *define* the sine and cosine of $\theta$, as follows:

$$
\cos\theta = x, \qquad \sin\theta = y
$$

In other words,

- the cosine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $x$-coordinate of $P$, and
- the sine of $\theta$ is defined to be equal to the $y$-coordinate of $P$.

This way, our trigonometric ratios make sense for any angle, even if this angle is larger than $90^\circ$." :tutorial/id #uuid "67345ec4-5f02-5d0a-9900-417059fb1ba3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6a1c1a6d-1eee-5229-b88d-9d28c1ae4c0a" :step/math-academy-id 40995 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060777}} {:db/id 17592186060777 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059830 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059389 :question/id #uuid "ec8644e2-c365-5dce-bb21-7a148203a03a" :question/math-academy-id "e-10818"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1810cacd-3565-5438-ae93-45b50970f5dd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050291}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060327} {:db/id 17592186060328}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Trigonometric Ratio Given a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "c87cdc7f-1883-5d6b-8cb5-f78979ccbb35" :step/math-academy-id 40996 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060739}} {:db/id 17592186060778 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060972 :tutorial/content "We can calculate a trigonometric ratio of *any* angle $\theta$ by finding the ratio of the corresponding reference angle and adjusting the sign depending on which quadrant our angle lies in.

To do this, we perform the following steps:

1. Find the reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the ratio for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting ratio is positive or negative.

We must do the last step because the ratio for $\theta_R$ will always be nonnegative, but the ratio for $\theta$ may not be.

But how do we determine whether the ratio for $\theta$ is positive or negative? This depends on the trigonometric ratio and which quadrant the angle is in.

To help us remember when various trigonometric ratios are positive, we use the mnemonic "**A**ll **S**tudents **T**ake **C**alculus."

- **A**ll of the trigonometric ratios are positive in quadrant I
- **S**ine (and only sine) is positive in quadrant II
- **T**angent (and only tangent) is positive in quadrant III
- **C**osine (and only cosine) is positive in quadrant IV

We can represent this in a so-called CAST diagram, shown below.

![](images/9a/9a6d43985058f1afd33272537def49886177aceab115f0084b1cf9d08ba78c43.png)

For example, let's consider $\sin 140^\circ$.

![](images/da/da7ca1a89b91d157ad97a3800d8c2d67efb467a8ceaa8f3c964bea5275ecfc5d.png)

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = 140^\circ
$$

is the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= 180^{∘} - θ \\
&= 180^{∘} - 140^{∘} \\
&= 40^{∘}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\sin{140^\circ}$, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\sin\theta_R = \sin{40^\circ}
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\sin{140^\circ}$ must be *positive* because the sine ratio is *always* positive in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin 140^\circ = \sin{40^\circ}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "807bb7a1-70c9-500c-be69-53b15b903672" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6763 :tutorial/title "The CAST Diagram"} :step/id #uuid Let $P'$ be the image of $P$ under a reflection across the $y$-axis. This gives a pair of congruent angles of measure $45^\circ$, as shown.

![](images/c4/c4875682498edaadc74a8af238fdf3293b4820025256df78e60867940061785e.png)

According to the definition, $\cos(135^\circ)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$. But this is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point $P'$ *taken with the opposite sign.*

The $x$-coordinate of $P'$ equals the cosine of the reference angle.

$$
\cos(45^\circ)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\cos(\, \underbrace{135^\circ}_{\theta} \,) =-\cos(\, \underbrace{45^\circ}_{\theta_R} \,) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

So, we simplified the evaluation of $\cos(135^\circ)$ by evaluating the cosine of the corresponding reference angle

$$
\theta_R=45^\circ
$$

*with an additional sign adjustment* for the final result.

We can use a similar argument to show that, since

$$
y = \sin\theta
$$

we have

$$
\sin(135^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}
$$

In this case, we do **NOT** change the sign because the $y$-coordinates of $P'$ and $P$ *are equal.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "8c1461a2-d5b4-5d11-b0ad-6537ca726992" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10532 :tutorial/title "Calculating Trigonometric Ratios Using Reference Angles"} :step/id #uuid "bdeb7825-3a44-52de-9875-55a1ffbcd7e7" :step/math-academy-id 210844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060778}} {:db/id 17592186060861 :tutorial/content "We can use reference angles to evaluate trigonometric ratios for angles outside the first quadrant.

To demonstrate, let's determine the value of $\cos (135^\circ)$, corresponding to the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the unit circle, as shown below.

![](images/be/bef50a070785e4bb86867ba6404942fd7eaa04b60720adfb04176bafe2fa2121.png)

$$
\theta=135^\circ

is

$$

Let $P'$ be the image of $P$ under a reflection across the $y$-axis. This gives a pair of congruent angles of measure $45^\circ$, as shown.

![](images/c4/c4875682498edaadc74a8af238fdf3293b4820025256df78e60867940061785e.png)

According to the definition, $\cos(135^\circ)$ is the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$. But this is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point $P'$ *taken with the opposite sign.*

The $x$-coordinate of $P'$ equals the cosine of the reference angle.

$$
\cos(45^\circ)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\cos(\, \underbrace{135^\circ}_{\theta} \,) =-\cos(\, \underbrace{45^\circ}_{\theta_R} \,) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
$$

So, we simplified the evaluation of $\cos(135^\circ)$ by evaluating the cosine of the corresponding reference angle

$$

$$

*with an additional sign adjustment* for the final result.

We can use a similar argument to show that, since

$$
y = \sin\theta
$$

we have

$$
